lesson.title: Filling in the Blanks: What Arguments Are
lesson.summary: Arguments are the actual values you supply inside the parentheses of a function call, and Python matches them to the function's parameters, either by position or by name, to run the body with real data.
lesson.body:
A function call like rectangle_area(4, 9) supplies two arguments: 4 and 9. These are the actual, concrete values handed to the function at the moment it is called, in contrast to the parameters width and height, which are just the placeholder names written into the function's definition, waiting for something to fill them. It is worth holding this distinction firmly: parameters live in the def line and never change once the function is written, while arguments are chosen fresh at every single call and can be different every time. Saying "the function has two parameters" describes the function's design; saying "this call passes two arguments" describes one specific use of it.

Python's default way of matching arguments to parameters is positional: the first argument fills the first parameter, the second argument fills the second parameter, and so on, purely based on the order each appears. This is exactly how function calls work under the hood, as covered when function calls were introduced: the call transfers control into the body with each parameter already bound to its matching argument, left to right. With def rectangle_area(width, height): return width * height, calling rectangle_area(4, 9) binds width to 4 and height to 9, computing 4 * 9 which is 36. Because matching is positional by default, the number of arguments must correspond to the number of parameters; calling rectangle_area(4) with only one argument raises a TypeError, since Python has no value to bind to height, and calling rectangle_area(4, 9, 2) raises a TypeError as well, since there is no third parameter to receive the extra 2.

Python also supports keyword arguments, where you name which parameter each value belongs to directly in the call, using parameter_name=value. This frees you from relying on position. Calling rectangle_area(height=9, width=4) produces the exact same result as rectangle_area(4, 9), namely 36, even though the order in the call is reversed, because each value explicitly states which parameter it is meant to fill rather than relying on left to right order. Keyword arguments become especially valuable once a function has many parameters, since a call like build_profile(name="Lin", age=17, grade=11) is far easier to read and far less error prone than build_profile("Lin", 17, 11), where a reader has to remember, or go check, what each position is supposed to mean.

Tracing a mixed example ties this together. Suppose def describe(item, price): return item + " costs $" + str(price). Calling describe("pencil", 1) uses positional arguments, binding item to "pencil" and price to 1, and returns 'pencil costs $1'. Calling describe(price=1, item="pencil") uses keyword arguments instead, arrives at the identical binding despite the reversed order in the call, and returns the identical string. Both calls are valid and both produce the same result, because in each case Python's job is the same: connect every argument to the correct parameter before the function body starts running, whether that connection is made by counting positions or by reading explicit names.
